title: No vision grasps Him
hook: eyes do not comprehend Him, and He comprehends all vision (6:103)

segments.voice: Yesterday: seed and stone split open. Your line was the seed splits. Did something get planted, or watered? Today, a verse about eyes, and what they can't hold. Day four hundred two.
screen: `SEED AND STONE SPLIT OPEN — THE SEED SPLITS.`

segments.voice: Try to see your own eyes. Not in a mirror, that's a reflection. Directly. You can't. The thing you see with is the one thing you can never look at. Now try the other direction: try to take in the whole ocean from a beach. Your eyes give up at the horizon. Human sight is a wonderful tool, and it has edges on both sides. Surah six has just walked through stars, seeds and dawn, all things you can see. And then, verse one-oh-three, it names the one thing sight can't reach.
screen: `TRY TO SEE YOUR OWN EYES.` → `THE OCEAN ENDS AT THE HORIZON.` → `WHAT SIGHT CAN'T REACH.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision. He is the Subtile, the Aware.” The Arabic verb is adraka: to reach, to overtake, to catch up with and take in completely. Eyes don't catch up with Allah. Allah catches up with every eye. And the two names at the end fit. Al-Latif: the subtle, so fine He passes beneath notice, and also the gentle, the kind. Al-Khabir: the one who knows the inside of things. This verse has a long history in Muslim thought. Aishah, the Prophet's wife, recited it when someone asked whether the Prophet ﷺ had seen his Lord on the Night Journey; her answer, in Bukhari, was no, though other companions, Ibn Abbas among them, are reported to have held a different view. Scholars have also asked about the next life. Many Sunni scholars hold that believers will see Allah in the hereafter, citing a verse in surah seventy-five about faces looking toward their Lord, and a hadith comparing it to seeing the full moon. They read today's verse as saying eyes can't encompass Him, not that they can never see. Mu'tazili theologians and Twelver Shia scholars read the verse as ruling out seeing God with eyes at all, and understand those other texts in another way. The schools differ. All of them agree on the second half: He sees every eye. A famous hadith, in which Jibril asks the Prophet about faith, describes the highest level, ihsan, as worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, knowing that He sees you.
screen: `ADRAKA — TO REACH AND TAKE IN.` · `AL-LATIF, AL-KHABIR.` · `WILL HE BE SEEN? THE SCHOOLS DIFFER.` · `IHSAN — HE SEES YOU.` · then, large: `VISION COMPREHENDETH HIM NOT.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and close your eyes. Notice that you've switched off the main way you take in the world. Your hearing gets louder. Your body gets heavier. Now, without opening your eyes, rest in the second half of the verse. You can't see Him. He sees you. Not as a camera, not as a judge on a screen. As the subtle one, the gentle one, who knows the inside. Breathe in that. The bell holds the time.
No vision grasps Him. Eyes don't take Allah in, but He takes in every eye: the Subtle, the Aware. Today's word.
Your line: seen by the unseen. Today, once, when no one's watching, remember that you're still seen, and act like it, gently. Day four hundred two.

howItsDone: Muslims cite 6:103 in teaching that Allah is beyond physical sight, and the hadith of Jibril's definition of ihsan, worship as though you see Him, for He sees you, is among the most taught texts on sincerity in prayer.

original.note: Arabic: eyes do not reach Him (6:103).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is invisible.
what it means: eyes can't reach or take in Allah, but He takes in every eye, subtly and gently.

what a scholar hears: the verse sits at the center of the ru'yah debate: Ash'aris and Atharis distinguish seeing from encompassing (idrak); Mu'tazilis and Twelver Shia scholars cite it to deny ocular vision.
